subject: history
title: The Meiji Restoration (1868–1912): how Japan remade the state, built a conscript army, sent diplomats to study the West, and became an imperial power
dek: In January 1868 young samurai seized the imperial palace, declared the shogunate ended, and announced rule would return to the emperor. What followed was not a single day of restoration but four decades of state-building: the Charter Oath, abolition of the domains, conscription, the Iwakura Mission, industrialization, a constitution, wars with China and Russia, and the annexation of Korea. When Emperor Meiji died in 1912, Japan was a great power. The transformation was violent, deliberate, and uneven—not inevitable, not Western imitation, and not complete until empire followed reform.

thumb.alt: Formal photograph of Emperor Meiji in 1872, wearing traditional court dress.

hero.alt: Emperor Meiji in formal court attire, photographed by Uchida Kuichi in 1872.
hero.caption: Emperor Meiji in 1872, photographed by Uchida Kuichi. He was fifteen when the Restoration coup happened in 1868, and he reigned until 1912. The Meiji era is named after his reign name, meaning 'enlightened rule.' The reforms happened in his name, though the genrō oligarchs—Ōkubo, Kido, Itō—wielded executive power for most of his reign.

honesty: The Meiji Restoration names both a coup (the January 1868 seizure of the palace and the end of Tokugawa rule) and a multi-decade process of state transformation ending with Emperor Meiji's death in 1912. It is not a single day, not a spontaneous uprising by peasants or merchants, and not only domestic reform—by 1894–95 Japan had defeated Qing China, by 1904–05 it had defeated Russia, and by 1910 it had annexed Korea. This capsule focuses on how the Meiji state was built—domains abolished, conscription imposed, missions sent abroad, industries founded, a constitution written—before expanding into empire. The wars with China (1894–95) and Russia (1904–05) are named as turning points but not narrated in detail; they belong to After, not to the core question of how Japan remade its own state. Casualty figures for the Satsuma Rebellion (1877) and later conflicts vary across sources; this capsule uses scholarly estimates and notes uncertainty. The genrō (elder statesmen) who actually governed are named, because Emperor Meiji reigned but did not rule in the executive sense until late in his life. Earlier Capsules lessons (May Fourth, Partition of India, Haitian Revolution) are cited as examples of other state crises where dates and sovereignty were contested, not as comparisons.

timeline.label: Perry's black ships
timeline.detail: Commodore Matthew Perry of the United States Navy arrived with a fleet demanding Japan open to trade. The Tokugawa shogunate, which had enforced a policy of near-isolation (sakoku) since the 1630s, faced a crisis it could not resolve by force. Perry returned in 1854; the Treaty of Kanagawa opened two ports.

timeline.label: Ansei treaties
timeline.detail: The shogunate signed commercial treaties with the United States, Britain, France, Russia, and the Netherlands—unequal treaties granting extraterritoriality and limiting Japanese tariff autonomy. These treaties, negotiated without imperial approval, deepened political crisis and fueled sonnō jōi ('revere the emperor, expel the barbarians') activism among lower samurai.

timeline.label: Bakumatsu violence
timeline.detail: The late Tokugawa period (bakumatsu) saw assassinations, foreign attacks on Japanese radicals, and punitive Western naval bombardments (Kagoshima 1863, Shimonoseki 1864). Chōshū and Satsuma domains, once shogunal enemies, began cooperating against the Tokugawa after defeats taught them that expelling foreigners by force was impossible.

timeline.label: Restoration coup / Boshin War begins
timeline.detail: On 3 January 1868 (Keiō 3/12/9 in the old calendar), Satsuma and Chōshū forces seized the imperial palace in Kyoto and declared the 'restoration' of imperial rule. The Boshin War (1868–69) followed; Tokugawa loyalists were defeated. Edo (renamed Tokyo) surrendered in May 1868. This is the political Restoration—the end of the shogunate.

timeline.label: Charter Oath
timeline.detail: Emperor Meiji promulgated the Charter Oath (Gokajō no Goseimon), a five-article statement of governing principles drafted by court nobles and samurai reformers. It promised deliberative assemblies, unity of purpose, abandonment of 'evil customs,' knowledge sought throughout the world, and strengthening the imperial polity. Vague but symbolically crucial.

timeline.label: Daimyō return their domains
timeline.detail: Former daimyō (domain lords) were pressured to return their land registers to the emperor. This hanseki hōkan was the first step toward abolishing the domain system; the daimyō became governors of their former lands, now officially imperial provinces.

timeline.label: Abolition of the domains (haihan chiken)
timeline.detail: The Meiji government abolished the 260-odd domains (han) and replaced them with centrally administered prefectures (ken). Former samurai lost stipends tied to domains; the central government assumed their debts and paid them off in bonds. This was the administrative Restoration—centralization of power.

timeline.label: Iwakura Mission
timeline.detail: A delegation of 50 officials (including Iwakura Tomomi, Ōkubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi, and Itō Hirobumi) toured the United States and Europe for nearly two years, observing governments, industries, schools, and militaries. They returned convinced that Japan needed gradual constitutional development and that renegotiating the unequal treaties required proof of 'civilization.'

timeline.label: Conscription ordinance
timeline.detail: The government introduced universal male conscription, creating a national army that did not rely on samurai status. The ordinance declared all men equal in the duty to defend the nation—a radical break from hereditary warrior privilege. Peasant riots protested the 'blood tax.'

timeline.label: Korean expedition debate / Ōkubo-Saigō split
timeline.detail: Saigō Takamori and others argued for a military expedition to Korea (seikanron). Ōkubo and the Iwakura Mission returnees opposed it, arguing Japan was not ready. Saigō and allies resigned from the government. This split led to the Satsuma Rebellion four years later.

timeline.label: Satsuma Rebellion
timeline.detail: Saigō Takamori led disaffected samurai in Satsuma (Kyushu) in revolt against the Meiji government. The new conscript army defeated them after six months of fighting; Saigō died at the Battle of Shiroyama in September 1877. This was the last major samurai rebellion; the conscript army had proven itself.

timeline.label: Industrialization and infrastructure
timeline.detail: The government built model factories (Tomioka Silk Mill, shipyards, arsenals), imported foreign experts, sent students abroad, and later privatized many enterprises to favored merchant houses (zaibatsu). Railroads, telegraph, postal systems, and banks were established. The slogan fukoku kyōhei ('rich country, strong army') summarized the strategy.

timeline.label: Promulgation of the Meiji Constitution
timeline.detail: Emperor Meiji promulgated the Constitution of the Empire of Japan, drafted largely by Itō Hirobumi after study of the Prussian model. It established a bicameral Diet, but sovereignty rested with the emperor, not the people. The prime minister and cabinet were responsible to the emperor, not the Diet. Subjects had rights 'within the limits of law.'

timeline.label: First Diet session
timeline.detail: The Imperial Diet convened for the first time in November 1890. The House of Representatives was elected by a narrow franchise (about 1% of the population, based on tax qualifications); the House of Peers included titled nobility and imperial appointees. Political parties formed and began contesting budgets and policies.

timeline.label: First Sino-Japanese War
timeline.detail: Japan and Qing China went to war over influence in Korea. Japan won decisively; the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895) forced China to recognize Korean independence, cede Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula, and pay indemnity. European powers intervened (Triple Intervention) to force Japan to return Liaodong, but the victory announced Japan as a regional power.

timeline.label: Anglo-Japanese Alliance
timeline.detail: Britain and Japan signed a military alliance, the first between a European great power and an Asian state on equal terms. It recognized Japan's interests in Korea and China and provided mutual defense guarantees. The alliance reflected Japan's arrival as a diplomatic peer.

timeline.label: Russo-Japanese War
timeline.detail: Japan and Russia fought over Manchuria and Korea. Japan won battles at Port Arthur, Mukden, and Tsushima Strait, but the war strained Japanese finances and casualties were high. The Treaty of Portsmouth (1905), mediated by U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt, gave Japan control of Korea, southern Sakhalin, and the Liaodong lease, but no indemnity. Domestic riots protested the 'weak' treaty.

timeline.label: Annexation of Korea
timeline.detail: Japan formally annexed Korea, ending the Korean Empire. Korea became a Japanese colony, ruled by a Governor-General. Korean resistance continued underground and later erupted in the 1919 March First Movement. This was the culmination of Japan's imperial expansion during the Meiji era.

timeline.label: Death of Emperor Meiji
timeline.detail: Emperor Meiji died at age 59. His reign had lasted 45 years; the Meiji era ended. General Nogi Maresuke and his wife committed ritual suicide (junshi) on the day of the funeral. The Taishō era began under Emperor Taishō (Yoshihito), but the genrō oligarchs still held power.

fun_fact.title: The Iwakura Mission spent nearly two years abroad and missed the domestic crisis
fun_fact.text: The Iwakura Mission (1871–73) took 50 officials, including some of the most powerful men in the Meiji government, out of Japan for 22 months. While they toured American railroads, British shipyards, and Prussian military academies, Japan faced a domestic political crisis: Saigō Takamori and his allies were pushing for war with Korea. When the mission returned in 1873, Ōkubo Toshimichi and Kido Takayoshi sided against Saigō, leading to his resignation. The mission's observations shaped the decision to oppose the Korean expedition and to write a constitution—but it nearly cost them control of the government while they were gone.

glossary.explain: Both the January 1868 coup that ended Tokugawa shogunal rule and the broader process of state-building (1868–1912) that centralized power, abolished domains, built a conscript army, industrialized, and wrote a constitution. Not a single day; not a popular uprising.

Emperor of Japan from 1867 to 1912 (1852–1912). He was fifteen at the time of the Restoration coup. The Meiji era is named after his reign name, meaning 'enlightened rule.' He reigned but did not personally govern; the genrō oligarchs wielded executive power.
The late Tokugawa period, roughly 1853–1868, from Perry's arrival to the Restoration coup. A time of political crisis, foreign pressure, and internal violence.
The military government that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868, led by the Tokugawa family of shoguns. Ended by the Meiji Restoration coup.
The Tokugawa policy (from the 1630s to 1850s) of severely restricting foreign contact, allowing trade only through Nagasaki with the Dutch and Chinese. Perry's 1853 arrival forced its end.

United States Navy commodore (1794–1858) who commanded the 1853–54 expedition to Japan, demanding trade relations. His 'black ships' (steam-powered warships) symbolized Western military superiority and forced the opening of Japan.
Treaty signed 31 March 1854 between the United States and Japan, opening the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate and granting most-favored-nation status. The first of the unequal treaties.

The 1858 commercial treaties between Japan and Western powers (US, Britain, France, Russia, Netherlands) that granted extraterritoriality (foreigners tried under their own laws) and limited Japanese tariff autonomy. Renegotiating them became a major Meiji goal; full revision was not achieved until 1911.

aliases: revere the emperor, expel the barbarians
glossary.explain: Political slogan of the 1860s meaning 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians.' Lower samurai activists used it to oppose the shogunate's compromises with foreigners. After Western military power was demonstrated, the movement shifted from expelling to learning from the West.
Southwestern domain (modern Yamaguchi Prefecture) that led anti-Tokugawa activism in the 1860s and was a core power base of the Meiji government. Kido Takayoshi and Itō Hirobumi were Chōshū men.

Southwestern domain (modern Kagoshima Prefecture) that allied with Chōshū against the Tokugawa. Ōkubo Toshimichi and Saigō Takamori were Satsuma men. The Satsuma Rebellion (1877) was the last major samurai revolt.

The civil war (1868–69) between the new Meiji government (backed by Satsuma and Chōshū) and Tokugawa loyalists. Edo surrendered in May 1868; the last Tokugawa forces were defeated in Hokkaido in 1869.

Five-article statement promulgated by Emperor Meiji on 6 April 1868, outlining governing principles: deliberative assemblies, unity, abandonment of 'evil customs,' seeking knowledge worldwide, and strengthening the polity. Vague but symbolically foundational.
August 1871 abolition of the feudal domains (han) and their replacement with centrally administered prefectures (ken). The administrative Restoration—the real centralization of power.
Feudal lords who ruled domains under the Tokugawa system. In 1869–71 they were pressured to return their domains to the emperor and lost their autonomous authority.

Hereditary warrior class in Tokugawa Japan. The Meiji government abolished samurai legal privileges, ended stipends, and banned wearing swords (1876). Many became officers in the new army or bureaucrats; some rebelled.

January 1873 law introducing universal male conscription, creating a national army not based on samurai status. Declared all men equal in the duty to defend the nation. Peasants rioted, calling it the 'blood tax.'

1871–73 diplomatic mission to the United States and Europe, led by Iwakura Tomomi and including Ōkubo, Kido, and Itō. Spent 22 months observing governments, industries, schools, militaries. Returned convinced Japan needed gradual constitutional development and industrial strength before renegotiating the unequal treaties.
Court noble (1825–1883) who helped orchestrate the Restoration coup and led the 1871–73 mission to the West. Represented the imperial court faction within the Meiji oligarchy.

Satsuma samurai (1830–1878) who became the most powerful Meiji leader in the 1870s, opposing Saigō's Korean expedition and pushing centralization and industrialization. Assassinated in 1878 by disgruntled samurai.
Chōshū samurai (1833–1877) and key Restoration leader. Traveled on the Iwakura Mission; opposed the Korean expedition. Died in 1877 during the Satsuma Rebellion.

Satsuma samurai (1828–1877) who led the Restoration coup's military forces. Resigned in 1873 after the Korean expedition debate; led the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. Died at Shiroyama. Later remembered as a tragic hero.

Chōshū samurai (1841–1909) who traveled on the Iwakura Mission, drafted the Meiji Constitution (1889), and served four terms as prime minister. First Resident-General of Korea (1905–09); assassinated by Korean nationalist An Jung-geun in 1909.

1873 debate over whether to send a military expedition to Korea. Saigō and allies supported it; Ōkubo and the Iwakura Mission returnees opposed it, arguing Japan was not ready. Saigō lost and resigned, leading to the 1877 rebellion.

February–September 1877 samurai revolt in Kyushu led by Saigō Takamori against the Meiji government. The new conscript army defeated it. Saigō died at the Battle of Shiroyama (24 September 1877). The last major samurai rebellion.

Informal council of senior Meiji leaders (Itō, Yamagata, Matsukata, Inoue, and others) who wielded executive power behind the scenes, especially in choosing prime ministers. Not defined by the constitution; a carryover of oligarchic rule.
Slogan summarizing Meiji strategy: build a wealthy economy and a strong military to resist Western domination and achieve equality with the great powers.

Meiji-era slogan promoting Westernization in technology, education, dress, and customs. Associated with intellectuals like Fukuzawa Yukichi. Implied that Japan must adopt aspects of 'civilization' (i.e. Western modernity) to be taken seriously by the West.

Large industrial and financial conglomerates that emerged in Meiji Japan, often with government patronage. Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo, and Yasuda were the largest. Dominated the economy into World War II.

aliases: Constitution of the Empire of Japan
glossary.explain: Constitution promulgated 11 February 1889, drafted by Itō Hirobumi. Established a bicameral Diet, but sovereignty rested with the emperor. The cabinet was responsible to the emperor, not the legislature. Rights were granted 'within the limits of law.' Modeled partly on the Prussian constitution.

Bicameral legislature established by the 1889 Constitution, first convened 1890. House of Representatives elected by limited franchise (tax qualification); House of Peers composed of nobility and imperial appointees. Had budget approval power but limited ability to challenge executive.
Meiji intellectual (1835–1901) who wrote 'Encouragement of Learning' and other works advocating education, independence, and bunmei kaika. Founded Keio University. His face is on the 10,000-yen note.

War (1894–95) between Japan and Qing China over influence in Korea. Japan won decisively. Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895) forced China to recognize Korean independence, cede Taiwan and Liaodong, and pay indemnity. The Triple Intervention (Russia, Germany, France) forced Japan to return Liaodong.

Treaty ending the First Sino-Japanese War, signed 17 April 1895. China ceded Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula, recognized Korean independence, paid a large indemnity, and opened more treaty ports. Japan's victory shocked the world.

April 1895 diplomatic intervention by Russia, Germany, and France forcing Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula to China in exchange for additional indemnity. Japan complied but resented the humiliation, especially when Russia leased Liaodong (Port Arthur) from China three years later.

Alliance signed 30 January 1902 between Britain and Japan, the first between a European great power and an Asian state on equal terms. Mutual defense pact; recognized Japan's interests in Korea and China. Lasted until 1923.

War (1904–05) between Japan and Russia over Manchuria and Korea. Japan won battles at Port Arthur, Mukden, and Tsushima Strait, but the war was costly. Treaty of Portsmouth (1905) gave Japan control of Korea, southern Sakhalin, and the Liaodong lease. No indemnity; domestic riots in Tokyo protested the 'weak' peace.

Treaty ending the Russo-Japanese War, signed 5 September 1905 in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, mediated by U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt. Japan gained control of Korea, southern Sakhalin, and the Liaodong lease, but no indemnity. Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize; Japan's public was furious.

Japan formally annexed Korea on 22 August 1910, ending the Korean Empire. Korea became a colony under a Governor-General. Colonial rule lasted until 1945. Koreans resisted; the 1919 March First Movement was violently suppressed.

1912–1926, the reign of Emperor Taishō (Yoshihito), son of Emperor Meiji. Known for brief experiments in party politics ('Taishō Democracy') before militarism and authoritarianism returned in the 1930s.

General (1849–1912) who led Japanese forces at Port Arthur during the Russo-Japanese War. On the day of Emperor Meiji's funeral (13 September 1912), he and his wife committed ritual suicide (junshi) to follow the emperor in death—a gesture that shocked modernizing Japan.

Legal privilege granted by the unequal treaties allowing foreign nationals in Japan to be tried under their own country's laws rather than Japanese law. A humiliation Japan worked to end; full treaty revision was achieved only in 1899–1911.
Feudal domains ruled by daimyō under the Tokugawa system. There were about 260 han in 1868. Abolished in August 1871 and replaced with prefectures.
Centrally administered territorial units that replaced the feudal domains in 1871. Modern Japan is still organized into prefectures.

1869 process in which daimyō were pressured to 'return' their land registers to the emperor, nominally surrendering their domains. They were then reappointed as governors. A transitional step before full abolition of the domains in 1871.

sections.title: A shogunate, two centuries of isolation, and the black ships that forced the question no one knew how to answer

blocks.text: In 1853 Japan was not waiting for Perry. The Tokugawa shogunate had ruled since 1603, maintaining a policy of sakoku—near-total isolation—since the 1630s. Foreign trade was limited to a Dutch outpost and Chinese merchants at Nagasaki. The shogun governed from Edo (modern Tokyo); the emperor in Kyoto was a ceremonial figure with no executive power. Daimyō ruled 260-odd domains, each with its own samurai bureaucracy. The system had brought peace and stability for two centuries, but it had also frozen social roles: samurai on top, peasants farming, merchants at the legal bottom despite their wealth. Traveling abroad was punishable by death.

When Commodore Matthew Perry arrived in July 1853 with four warships—two steam-powered 'black ships'—and a letter from U.S. President Millard Fillmore demanding trade relations, the shogunate faced a crisis it had no script for. Perry said he would return the next year for an answer. The shogunate consulted the daimyō, an unprecedented admission of weakness. Some argued for war; others saw that Japan's coastal defenses and sailing ships could not defeat steam-powered fleets. Perry returned in February 1854 with more ships. The Treaty of Kanagawa, signed 31 March 1854, opened two ports and granted the United States most-favored-nation status. It was not a fair negotiation—it was a concession extracted by the threat of force.

blocks.alt: Portrait of Commodore Matthew Calbraith Perry in U.S. Navy uniform.
blocks.caption: Commodore Matthew Calbraith Perry (1794–1858), commander of the U.S. Navy expedition that forced Japan to open to trade in 1853–54. His 'black ships' (steam-powered warships) symbolized Western technological and military superiority. The Treaty of Kanagawa he negotiated was the first of the unequal treaties that shaped Meiji foreign policy.

blocks.text: The 1858 Ansei treaties with the United States, Britain, France, Russia, and the Netherlands went further: they granted foreigners extraterritoriality (tried under their own laws, not Japan's) and limited Japan's ability to set its own tariffs. The shogunate signed these treaties without imperial approval, angering court nobles and samurai who rallied under the slogan sonnō jōi—'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians.' The 1860s became a decade of assassinations, anti-foreigner violence, and punitive Western naval bombardments of Japanese ports (Kagoshima 1863, Shimonoseki 1864). Lower samurai from southwestern domains—especially Satsuma and Chōshū—learned that expelling the West by force was impossible. The question shifted from 'how do we keep them out' to 'how do we catch up.' The shogunate, unable to unify the domains or resist the foreign powers, lost legitimacy. By 1867 the slogan sonnō jōi no longer meant expelling foreigners—it meant overthrowing the shogun in the emperor's name.

sections.title: A coup in January 1868, the Charter Oath, forty years of state-building, and the wars that followed

blocks.text: On 3 January 1868 (Keiō 3, twelfth month, ninth day in the old calendar), forces from Satsuma, Chōshū, and allied domains seized the imperial palace in Kyoto and declared the 'restoration' of imperial rule. Emperor Meiji, fifteen years old, was the symbol; the real power lay with samurai leaders like Ōkubo Toshimichi, Saigō Takamori, and Kido Takayoshi. The shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, had already announced his resignation in November 1867, hoping to retain influence in a new council structure. The coup cut him out. The Boshin War followed: a civil conflict between the new Meiji government and Tokugawa loyalists. Edo surrendered in May 1868 without a siege; the city was renamed Tokyo ('eastern capital'), and the emperor moved there from Kyoto. The last Tokugawa forces were defeated in Hokkaido in mid-1869. This was the political Restoration—the end of the shogunate.

On 6 April 1868, Emperor Meiji promulgated the Charter Oath (Gokajō no Goseimon), a five-article statement of principles. It promised that 'deliberative assemblies shall be widely established,' that 'all classes, high and low, shall unite,' that 'evil customs of the past shall be broken off,' that 'knowledge shall be sought throughout the world,' and that 'the foundations of imperial rule shall be strengthened.' The language was vague and open to interpretation. There was no talk yet of constitutions, parliaments, or rights. It was a declaration that change was coming, that Japan would not be frozen in Tokugawa patterns, and that foreign knowledge—once forbidden—was now policy.

The real Restoration was administrative, not symbolic. In 1869 the daimyō were pressured to 'return' their domains to the emperor (hanseki hōkan). In August 1871 the government abolished the 260-odd domains entirely and replaced them with centrally administered prefectures (haihan chiken). Former samurai lost the stipends tied to their domains; the central government assumed the debts and paid them off in bonds. This was the end of feudalism—not by revolution from below, but by decree from above. Samurai were no longer a legally privileged class; the 1876 ban on wearing swords made that literal. Many became army officers, police, teachers, or bureaucrats. Some rebelled.

In January 1873 the government issued a conscription ordinance: universal male military service. The decree declared that 'the people are all equal' and that defending the nation was a duty, not a privilege. This was a radical break from the Tokugawa order, where only samurai bore arms. Peasants rioted, calling conscription the 'blood tax,' but the policy held. By 1877 the new army numbered over 40,000 men; when tested in the Satsuma Rebellion that year, it won. The conscript army proved that Japan no longer needed a samurai caste. The victory also meant that the state could enforce its will against regional warlords and disaffected elites.

blocks.alt: Group photograph of the Iwakura Mission members in Western dress, 1872.
blocks.caption: The Iwakura Mission, photographed in 1872. Seated center: Iwakura Tomomi. From left: Kido Takayoshi, Yamaguchi Masuka, Iwakura, Itō Hirobumi, Ōkubo Toshimichi. This mission spent nearly two years (1871–73) in the United States and Europe observing governments, industries, schools, and militaries. Their experiences shaped the decision to write a constitution and to oppose hasty foreign wars.

blocks.text: Between 1871 and 1873 a delegation of 50 officials toured the United States and Europe. The Iwakura Mission, led by court noble Iwakura Tomomi and including Ōkubo, Kido, and the young Itō Hirobumi, spent 22 months observing factories, railroads, navies, schools, parliaments, and courts. They returned convinced of two things: first, that Japan needed decades of internal development before it could renegotiate the unequal treaties or expand abroad; second, that a constitution and legal system modeled on Western examples—especially Prussia—would be necessary to prove Japan was 'civilized' and deserved equal treatment. This conclusion set them against Saigō Takamori and others who, in 1873, were pushing for a military expedition to Korea (seikanron). The debate split the government. Ōkubo and Kido opposed the expedition; Saigō lost and resigned. This was the break that led to the Satsuma Rebellion four years later.

Industrialization began with government investment in model factories, railroads, telegraph, and arsenals. The Tomioka Silk Mill (1872), naval shipyards, and weapons foundries were built with state funds and foreign technical advisors. Later many enterprises were sold to favored merchant houses—Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo—who became the zaibatsu conglomerates that dominated the economy. The slogan fukoku kyōhei ('rich country, strong army') summarized the strategy: build an industrial base to fund a modern military. Education expanded rapidly: compulsory elementary schooling was introduced in 1872, and thousands of students were sent abroad to study. By the 1880s Japan had railroads connecting Tokyo to Yokohama and Osaka, a postal system, banks, and newspapers. This was not organic development—it was state-directed transformation.

On 11 February 1889 Emperor Meiji promulgated the Constitution of the Empire of Japan. It had been drafted largely by Itō Hirobumi after years of study in Europe, especially Prussia. The constitution established a bicameral Diet—an elected House of Representatives and an appointed House of Peers—but sovereignty rested with the emperor, not the people. The cabinet and prime minister were responsible to the emperor, not the legislature. The Diet could approve or reject budgets, but if it rejected one, the previous year's budget remained in force. Rights were granted 'within the limits of law,' meaning they could be restricted by statute. The constitution was a gift from the emperor, not a contract with the people. It created a parliament, but not democracy. The first Diet convened in November 1890. Political parties formed and began contesting budgets, but the genrō—informal elder statesmen like Itō and Yamagata Aritomo—still controlled cabinet appointments and foreign policy behind the scenes.

By the 1890s the question was no longer whether Japan would survive foreign domination but whether it would dominate others. The First Sino-Japanese War (1894–95) began over influence in Korea. Japan defeated Qing China decisively on land and sea. The Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895) forced China to recognize Korean independence (effectively a Japanese protectorate), cede Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula, and pay a large indemnity. The victory shocked the world—an Asian power had beaten a traditional empire using Western military methods. The Triple Intervention (Russia, Germany, France) forced Japan to return Liaodong in exchange for more money, a humiliation compounded when Russia leased Port Arthur from China three years later. Japan prepared for the next war.

The Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) was fought over Manchuria and Korea. Japan won major battles—Port Arthur after a bloody siege, Mukden in Manchuria, and the annihilation of the Russian Baltic Fleet at Tsushima Strait in May 1905. But the war exhausted Japanese finances and manpower. The Treaty of Portsmouth (1905), mediated by U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt, gave Japan control of Korea, the southern half of Sakhalin Island, and the lease on Liaodong, but no indemnity. The Tokyo public rioted, furious at what they saw as a weak peace. Still, the war established Japan as a great power: the Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902) had already recognized it as Britain's Asian partner, and now the world saw that a modernized Asian state could defeat a European empire.

In 1910 Japan formally annexed Korea, ending the Korean Empire and making Korea a colony under a Governor-General. This was not the first act of Meiji imperialism, but it was the culmination. Emperor Meiji died on 30 July 1912 at age 59. General Nogi Maresuke, hero of Port Arthur, and his wife committed ritual suicide on the day of the emperor's funeral—junshi, following one's lord in death, a practice Meiji reformers thought they had abolished. The act shocked modernizing Japan and became a symbol of the tension between the new state and old loyalties. The Meiji era was over. Japan had gone from forced treaties to great-power status, from feudal domains to a centralized empire, from sakoku to colonial expansion. The transformation was deliberate, violent, and incomplete.

sections.title: The samurai who made the state, the emperor who reigned but did not rule, and the general who could not accept the new order

blocks.text: The Meiji Restoration was not the work of a single leader or a mass movement. It was a coup and a state-building project carried out by a small group of samurai from southwestern domains—Satsuma, Chōshū, Tosa, Hizen—who seized power in the emperor's name and then spent four decades centralizing that power, building institutions, and expanding abroad. Emperor Meiji reigned for 45 years but did not govern in the modern executive sense; the genrō oligarchs made the decisions. Ōkubo Toshimichi was the dominant figure of the 1870s before his assassination. Itō Hirobumi drafted the constitution and became the era's most visible statesman. Saigō Takamori, who helped make the Restoration, could not accept what it became and died leading a rebellion against it.

people.name: Emperor Meiji
people.alt: Emperor Meiji in formal court dress, 1872 photograph.
people.caption: Emperor Meiji in 1872, photographed by Uchida Kuichi. He was fifteen at the time of the Restoration coup. The era is named after his reign name, meaning 'enlightened rule.'
people.text: Born Mutsuhito, he became emperor at age fourteen in 1867, months before the Restoration coup. The young emperor was a symbol, not an executive. He was moved from Kyoto to Tokyo in 1868, renamed 'enlightened rule' (Meiji), and presented in official portraits as a modern monarch. He participated in state ceremonies, promulgated the Charter Oath and the Constitution, and declared wars, but the genrō oligarchs made policy. Only late in his reign did he assert personal views on appointments and treaties. When he died in 1912, millions mourned the Meiji era as a vanished golden age, even though many had suffered under its reforms.

people.name: Ōkubo Toshimichi
people.alt: Portrait photograph of Ōkubo Toshimichi in Western suit.
people.caption: Ōkubo Toshimichi, Satsuma samurai and the most powerful Meiji leader of the 1870s. Architect of centralization and industrialization; assassinated in 1878.
people.text: A Satsuma samurai, Ōkubo helped plan the Restoration coup and became the most powerful man in the Meiji government by the mid-1870s. He traveled with the Iwakura Mission (1871–73) and returned convinced that Japan needed decades of internal development before foreign expansion. He opposed Saigō's Korean expedition in 1873, leading to Saigō's resignation. Ōkubo pushed through domain abolition, conscription, and state-funded industrialization. He was often called the 'Bismarck of Japan' for his ruthless pragmatism. On 14 May 1878, he was assassinated by disgruntled samurai who blamed him for abandoning the old ways. His death left Itō Hirobumi as the next dominant figure.

people.name: Saigō Takamori
people.alt: Photograph of Saigō Takamori in kimono.
people.caption: Saigō Takamori, Satsuma general who led the Restoration's military forces and then led the 1877 rebellion against the state he had helped create.
people.text: A Satsuma samurai and military leader, Saigō commanded the forces that took Edo in 1868. He was beloved by soldiers and saw himself as defending samurai honor and the emperor's true will. In 1873 he advocated a military expedition to Korea (seikanron), arguing it would restore samurai purpose and expand Japanese influence. When Ōkubo and the Iwakura Mission returnees opposed him and the government voted against the plan, Saigō resigned and returned to Kagoshima. In February 1877, disaffected samurai rallied to him and began the Satsuma Rebellion. The Meiji army crushed it over six months; Saigō died at the Battle of Shiroyama on 24 September 1877. He became a tragic hero in popular memory—the last samurai, loyal to the end.

people.name: Itō Hirobumi
people.alt: Formal portrait of Itō Hirobumi in Western dress with medals.
people.caption: Itō Hirobumi, Chōshū samurai who drafted the Meiji Constitution (1889), served four terms as prime minister, and was assassinated in 1909.
people.text: Born a commoner in Chōshū, Itō was adopted into samurai status and joined anti-Tokugawa activism in the 1860s. He traveled to Britain in 1863 and saw industrialization firsthand. He was the youngest senior member of the Iwakura Mission (1871–73), where he studied constitutions and legal systems. Tasked with drafting Japan's constitution, he spent 1882–83 in Europe studying the Prussian model. The Constitution of the Empire of Japan (1889) was largely his work. He served as prime minister four times (1885–88, 1892–96, 1898, 1900–01) and was the dominant genrō figure after Ōkubo's death. He became the first Resident-General of Korea (1905–09), overseeing the transition to annexation. On 26 October 1909, he was assassinated at Harbin railway station by Korean nationalist An Jung-geun.

sections.title: The Iwakura Mission: two years abroad, and the decision that Japan was not ready for war

blocks.text: In November 1871, a delegation of 50 Japanese officials boarded a ship in Yokohama bound for San Francisco. The Iwakura Mission—named for its leader, court noble Iwakura Tomomi—included some of the most powerful men in the Meiji government: Ōkubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi, Itō Hirobumi (then 31 years old), and dozens of specialists and students. Their ostensible goal was to deliver diplomatic credentials to foreign heads of state and begin preliminary discussions on revising the unequal treaties. Their real purpose was broader: to observe how Western governments, militaries, industries, and schools actually worked. They would spend the next 22 months abroad—nearly two years away from Japan while the state they had just built was still fragile.

The mission spent four months in the United States, visiting factories, railroads, schools, Congress, and President Ulysses S. Grant. Ōkubo was struck by American industrial scale; Itō studied legal systems. In Britain they toured shipyards, textile mills, and the Houses of Parliament. In Prussia they watched military drills and met Bismarck. In France they observed the aftermath of the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune. They visited Belgium, the Netherlands, Russia, and more than a dozen other states. Everywhere they went, they took notes, collected documents, and asked how things were organized. This was not tourism—it was intelligence-gathering.

What they learned sobered them. Europe's industrial capacity dwarfed Japan's. Its railroads, telegraphs, and steamship networks moved goods and information faster than anything Japan had. Its armies used breech-loading rifles, Krupp artillery, and systematic staff planning. The mission also learned that the Western powers had no intention of revising the unequal treaties until Japan demonstrated it had adopted 'civilized' legal codes and governance—meaning constitutions, legal equality, and institutions that looked Western. The mission members realized that Japan could not yet negotiate as an equal and that attempting foreign expansion before building domestic strength would be disastrous.

While the mission was abroad, the government in Tokyo was debating what to do about Korea. Saigō Takamori and his allies argued for a military expedition (seikanron)—both to restore samurai purpose and to assert Japanese influence. Acting ministers, with Saigō's support, had tentatively decided to send him as an envoy to Korea, expecting the mission would be insulted and war would follow. When the Iwakura Mission returned in September 1873, Ōkubo and Kido moved immediately to reverse the decision. They argued that Japan could not afford a foreign war while it was still consolidating domestic control and building infrastructure. A heated cabinet meeting in October 1873 ended with the emperor (guided by the returned oligarchs) rejecting the Korean expedition. Saigō and his allies resigned and left Tokyo. The split was bitter and personal.

The consequences of the mission and the seikanron debate shaped the next four decades. The decision to prioritize domestic development over foreign adventure led to the conscription expansion, the focus on industry and education, and the deliberate approach to constitutional drafting. It also led to the Satsuma Rebellion (1877), because Saigō and other disaffected samurai believed the government had betrayed the Restoration's purpose. The mission's observations convinced Itō and others that Japan needed a constitution—not because they believed in democracy, but because they understood that the Western powers would not revise the unequal treaties without one. The Meiji Constitution (1889) was the direct result of lessons learned on the Iwakura Mission. So were the wars with China (1894–95) and Russia (1904–05): by the 1890s, Japan had built the strength Ōkubo said it needed in 1873, and it used that strength to expand exactly as Saigō had wanted two decades earlier—but on the state's terms, not his.

sections.title: German and Italian unification, American Reconstruction, Qing reform attempts, and Russian emancipation

blocks.text: The Meiji Restoration unfolded while other states were also remaking themselves or being remade. Germany unified under Prussian leadership after the Franco-Prussian War (1870–71); Bismarck's Reich became the model Itō Hirobumi studied when drafting the Meiji Constitution. Italy had unified in 1861 (completed with Rome in 1870), also creating a constitutional monarchy with a limited franchise. Both unifications, like Japan's, involved wars, centralization, and the abolition of older political units. Japan's oligarchs watched German industrialization and military organization closely and adapted what they saw.

In the United States, the Meiji Restoration coincided with Reconstruction (1865–77) following the Civil War. When the Iwakura Mission visited in 1872, they saw a country grappling with the aftermath of emancipation, constitutional amendments expanding citizenship, and violent resistance by former Confederates and white supremacist groups. Japanese observers noted the scale of American industry and railroads but also the instability of democratic politics. By 1877, when Reconstruction ended and federal troops withdrew from the South, the Satsuma Rebellion had just been crushed in Japan. Both countries were consolidating new orders after civil wars, but the U.S. was abandoning its experiment in racial equality while Japan was building a centralized authoritarian state.

Qing China was attempting its own reforms—the Tongzhi Restoration (1860s) and later the Self-Strengthening Movement—importing Western military technology and trying to preserve the dynasty by modernizing its military and administration. But the Qing reforms were slower, less centralized, and constrained by internal rebellions (Taiping, Nian, Dungan) and the entrenched power of regional governors. When Japan defeated China in 1894–95, the contrast was stark: Meiji Japan had centralized power, abolished feudal domains, and built a national army; Qing China had not. The defeat triggered more radical Chinese reform attempts (the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898) and eventually revolution (the Xinhai Revolution of 1911–12, covered in an earlier Capsules history lesson).

Russia under Tsar Alexander II had emancipated the serfs in 1861, roughly when Japan was in the late bakumatsu crisis. Russian reforms in the 1860s–70s introduced local councils (zemstva), modern courts, and military conscription—parallels to Meiji reforms. But Russian emancipation left peasants burdened with redemption payments and tied to village communes, and the tsarist state retained autocratic control. By the 1880s and 1890s, Russia and Japan were both expanding into East Asia—Russia pushing into Manchuria and seeking a warm-water port, Japan consolidating influence in Korea. The clash came in 1904–05, and Japan's victory shocked Europe: an Asian constitutional monarchy with a modern navy had defeated a European autocracy. The Russo-Japanese War's outcome inspired anti-colonial movements across Asia and helped trigger Russia's 1905 Revolution.

sections.title: Empire, Taishō democracy, and the long question of what the Restoration made

blocks.text: When Emperor Meiji died in 1912, Japan was a great power with colonies (Taiwan, Korea, southern Sakhalin), treaty ports in China, and a seat at the table of European diplomacy. The unequal treaties had been revised by 1911; extraterritoriality and tariff restrictions were gone. Japan had industrialized, built railroads and universities, written a constitution, and defeated two empires in war. It had also become an imperial power itself, ruling Korea as a colony and exerting influence in Manchuria. The Meiji transformation was real, but it was not the liberal, democratic path some early reformers had hoped for. The Constitution of 1889 created a parliament but reserved sovereignty to the emperor and left executive power with the genrō and the military, both of whom were outside parliamentary control.

The Taishō era (1912–26) is sometimes called the period of 'Taishō Democracy' because political parties briefly gained more influence over cabinets and budgets, and suffrage expanded (universal male suffrage in 1925). But the genrō still chose prime ministers, the military reported directly to the emperor, and the 1925 Peace Preservation Law criminalized 'dangerous thoughts'—meaning socialism, communism, or criticism of the imperial system. The democratic opening was real but fragile. By the 1930s, militarists and ultranationalists had reasserted control, using the emperor's sovereignty and the military's constitutional independence to justify expansion into Manchuria (1931), withdrawal from the League of Nations (1933), and eventually total war with China (1937) and the Pacific (1941–45).

The memory politics of the Meiji Restoration remain contested. In postwar Japan (after 1945), the Restoration was often taught as a modernization success story—how Japan escaped colonization by learning from the West and becoming a great power. But the same state-building process that created schools and railroads also created an emperor-centered ideology (kokutai), censorship, thought police, and colonial domination of Korea, Taiwan, and parts of China. Koreans remember the 1910 annexation and the colonial period (1910–45) as a national trauma; the March First Movement (1919) and later resistance are central to Korean national memory. The question 'what did the Meiji Restoration make?' has no single answer. It made a modern centralized state; it made an empire; it made the conditions for democracy and the conditions for fascism. It abolished feudalism and samurai privilege; it also built a military-industrial complex and an authoritarian constitution.

The Meiji oligarchs—Ōkubo, Kido, Itō, Yamagata—saw themselves as saving Japan from colonization. They succeeded in that narrow goal: Japan was never colonized. But the methods they used—rapid centralization, military expansion, thought control, empire-building—created new crises. The Pacific War (1941–45) ended with atomic bombs, occupation, and the dismantling of the Meiji constitutional system. The 1947 Constitution, written under U.S. occupation, made sovereignty reside in the people, not the emperor, and renounced war. The Meiji era ended in 1912, but the arguments about what it meant and what it cost are not over.

If the Iwakura Mission had not opposed the Korean expedition in 1873, or if Saigō Takamori had won the seikanron debate and Japan had gone to war with Korea in the 1870s, do you think Japan would still have followed the path of constitutional development and industrialization—or would early foreign expansion have derailed the centralization and state-building that later made Japan a great power?
